summary: The note surveys community tech programs across the US that tackle the digital divide by offering accessible technology education to all ages. It highlights programs for seniors, language-specific workshops, internet and device access, youth innovation, and public-private partnerships. It argues that digital literacy is a necessity and that closing the gap requires collective effort.
one_line: Community tech programs across the US are bridging the digital divide through accessible, inclusive technology education for people of all ages and backgrounds.
key_facts: Sandra Melendez launched "Tech Together" on October 10, 2023, in a community center in San Antonio, Texas.
A study as of September 2023 found that 36% of seniors are not proficient in basic digital skills.
"Silver Surfers," led by David Liu in Tampa, Florida, runs workshops for the elderly on using the internet and social media.
Miguel Rodriguez, 14, of New Haven, Connecticut, had to do homework on a cell phone before December 2023.
"Connect Community," launched by a coalition of tech volunteers, gave Miguel Rodriguez a laptop and free Wi-Fi.
"Code en Español" in Los Angeles, California, led by María Gomez, has offered bilingual tech workshops since early September 2023.
"Code en Español" teaches coding fundamentals, office applications, and internet safety to children and adults.
Jordan Harris started the "Youth Innovators" hub in Nashville, Tennessee, in late September 2023, where teens develop applications, explore robotics, and try virtual reality.
The nonprofit "Digitally Empowered" and the Cleveland, Ohio, local government opened multiple "Digital Hubs" offering lesson plans, tech support, and internship opportunities.
Grassroots movements and local governments provide free Wi-Fi spots and distribute donated devices to those in need.
The note argues bridging the divide requires a coalition of public, private, and nonprofit sectors.
